utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone this last day of the week. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to continue its examination of Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may Mr. Treanor be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it goes almost without saying that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, I nevertheless remind you to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe we concluded yesterday with your explanation of the backdrop to the founding of the SDS in 1990. May we turn then to the speech by Radovan Karadzic at the founding assembly, which will be shown on the screen in Sanction and can also be found in binder 1 at tab 1. Mr. Treanor, I note that portions of the speech have been highlighted. I presume those are the portions to which you wish to draw our attention. May I ask you then to discuss the aspects of that speech that you want to identify for the Court.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of Radovan Karadzic's opening statement at the founding assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party. In the speech he goes over the reasons for the founding of the party and its aims. We can pick out a few highlights here to give the Court an idea of his approach on this occasion. In the first paragraph, you can see that he says, among other things, he refers to the illusions which had been created, one of which was that the Serbian nation is small, weak, and insignificant. This deferred our friends and encouraged our enemies to begin finishing off the fragmented and dismembered Serbian nation. And further he says the dismembered -- that dismembered and divided during the war we continued divided in peacetime. We continue the genocide our enemies had carried out against us by destroying our own national and cultural identity. This is the sense of grievance that inspired the founding of the party. Further on in that page, I'd like to draw attention to another passage, in which he says: "Several hundred thousands of Serbs left Bosnia and Herzegovina in this period and Bosnia and Herzegovina was left without posterity. Territorial organisation broke down the natural Serbian entities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serbian nation was reduced to an inferior economic, demographic, and political position." Here he brings up two concerns which we'll be seeing coming to the fore time and again, that is, the demographic situation of the Serbian people in BH and the issue of the territorial division of BH. Dr. Karadzic and other people in the SDS felt that the territorial organisation of the republic, which was based on dividing the territory of the republic into administrative units known as municipalities, had been deliberately gerrymandered against the Serbs in order to prevent them from being a majority in many municipalities that -- in areas that they otherwise would have dominated. I think maybe we have one more passage here in the third page of the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]...page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, in this portion of the speech, is turning to the aims of the party. "The basic objective of the party is full and unconditional civil, national, cultural, religious and economic equality for the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Two paragraphs below that you see another passage not highlighted here, just the first sentence I'd like to read as one of the objectives of the party: "Is a federative Yugoslavia and in it an equal federal Bosnia and Herzegovina." This emerged as one of the most important points in the party programme and proved to be the crux of many of their activities over the coming months. I would remind the Court at this point that the SDA, the Bosnian Muslim party, the Party of Democratic Action, in its programme, recently adopted had favoured the continuance of Yugoslavia as a free community of republics within the boundaries that had been established within Yugoslavia and against any partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The HDZ, on the other hand, the Croatian Democratic Community, in its programmatic statement in August 1990 merely spoke of the right of the Croatian people to self-determination up to and including the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They didn't even mention Yugoslavia in their document. So the HDZ was clearly not providing a ringing endorsement to the continuation of Yugoslavia, whereas the SDA was willing to contemplate the continuance of BH within Yugoslavia, something which the SDS is very much coming out for here. I think we're finished with that document and we can now turn to the party programme as such, which embodies many of the points that were made in the speech as points in the official programme of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that document may be found in binder 1 at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could below up the first highlighted -- first two highlighted portions, maybe. Number 5: Equality as the basis of joint life. Equality was a very important term for the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party. That means the equality of the Serbian people within BH with the other peoples in BH. And 6, again we see the reference to Yugoslavia, a democratic Yugoslavia, structured as a modern federal state. Again, the word "federal" is a very important word for the Bosnian Serb leadership. There were arrangements under discussion which would have made Yugoslavia a confederal state rather than a federal. They were very much in favour of the maintenance of a federal state. The next highlighted portion, if we could blow that up. Again, repeating Bosnia-Herzegovina as an equal republic in a modern federal state. I think that's all we have on the programme. I think the main points have been brought out. Now I'd like to turn to the statute of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statute can be found at tab 4.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statute adopted in July 1990. We'll just go over a few general -- one or two general points here. I believe on page 3 of the original, Article 9 is something I'd like to call attention to. This refers to the -- as you can see, the rights and obligations of members of the party, including: "To obey party regulations and support the achievement of its goals and programme orientation and to implement and respect decisions of party organs." So party discipline was something that was required and expected. Now we'll briefly address the central organs of the party that were established by this statute. These are the party assembly, the party president, the Main Board, and the executive committee. Those are the ones we'll consider. The last two are less important. And at this point, I'd like to call the Court's attention to the fact that this statute was modified the following year, in July 1991, at the party's second assembly. Therefore, we will now consider the duties and responsibilities of the various party organs on the basis of that statute, since it was the statute in effect for the most important part of the period that we're concerned with in this presentation. The document you see before you is labelled a proposal. We do not possess a final copy of this document. However, it is apparent from the stenographic records of the second assembly of the SDS, which we have available, that this proposed statute was in fact adopted, with some very minor modifications. So this is the document that we base our discussion on. I would also observe that for the year intervening between the first party assembly and the second party assembly, we do not have very many documents from the SDS to indicate its internal operations. It is only after the second assembly where the volume of party documentation becomes significant. In fact, the second assembly in a certain sense marked an organisational rebirth of the party. They elected a new Main Board and Executive Board and started to get their own internal housekeeping, so to speak, in order. Many of the provisions in the two statutes are the same. I don't think we have anything else -- yes, I think we do. On page 5 of the original, Article 19. This addresses the issue of the hierarchical structure of the party. It states that the organisational forms of the SDS shall be an assembly and boards in local, municipal, city, and republican organisations. Now, those are the various levels of governance in the -- in BH, local meaning the local communities, the municipalities that I referred to, the cities, the city of Sarajevo, the only city in Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of administrative status, and of course the republic. The difference here between this statute and the original statute was that in 1990 there was reference to a regional -- regional boards of the party, which were party regions. This statute eliminates those party -- regional party boards. In fact, some of them continued to exist as -- Dr. Karadzic referred to them as coordinating bodies. So much for the territorial structure of the party. I think we can turn to the Article 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, does Article 30 address the rules and responsibilities of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We turn to the individual organs now. Article 30 deals with the Assembly and defines the Assembly as the highest organ of the SDS, and goes on to enumerate its responsibilities and the composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that can be found at page -- excuse me, Mr. Treanor. That can be found at page 11, under tab 5.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next we can go to Article 31. Article 31 contains a long list of the particular duties and responsibilities of the Assembly, including adopting and amending the programme, adopting Rules of Procedure, electing the presidents of the SDS, electing the Main Board, et cetera. Article 32 might be of some interest. Here we turn to the president of the party. This article defines the president of the SDS as the president of the Main Board as well, and stating the length of his mandate for four years. Then we have Article 32 and 33. Article 33 again contains another long list of the particular duties of the president of the party, including to represent the party, ensure the implementation of its programme, to convene the Assembly, convene sessions of the Main Board, coordinate the activities of organs and bodies of the party, take political and other decisions on behalf of the SDS, unless they are within the competence of the other organs, ensure the implementations of decisions of the party, et cetera. Now we turn to the Main Board. Article 35 defines the Main Board as the highest organ of the party between sessions of the Assembly of the party. Now, the Assembly of the party met once a year, so for the intervening year, the Main Board, according to the statute, is the highest organ of the party. If we can blow up Article 36. Article 36 specifies that the Main Board will have 45 members. This was a change from the 1990 statute, which had specified 52 members. And indicates that the Main Board will be elected by the Assembly from among its members, taking into account a territorial representation. And then we have 30, Article 37, which again is the long list of the particular duties of the Main Board, which include electing the president and two thirds of the members of the Executive Board of the party, preparing decisions to be adopted by the Assembly, deciding on the territorial organisation of the party, implementing decisions of the Assembly, considering and adopting reports of the Executive Board, et cetera. Now then we turn to the Executive Board, which is the last of the central party organs that we will consider here. In Article 39 - it's on page 11 of the statute - the Executive Board is described as having 15 members, some elected from the Main Board and some appointed on the basis of a nomination by the president of the party, and the Main Board is to have its own president. Then we have Article 41. We skipped Article 41, which I think we can conclude with this discussion, which again is the list of the particular duties of the Executive Board. The Executive Board is more of a managerial body rather than a policy making body which the Main Board is, and its duties include preparing materials for the needs of the Main Board, adopting its own Rules of Procedure, ensuring the implementation of the decisions of the Main Board, adopting commissions and appointing commissions and other working bodies, et cetera, including control of the SDS, of SDS property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, before we leave those articles, can I ask you briefly to turn to Article 49 and describe its relevance to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Article 49, as the Court can see, refers to the establishment of councils as advisory bodies of the SDS. These are not party organs per se. They are groups of individuals which are available for consultation by the party leadership. At various periods of time, we will see reference to a political council, an economic council, and indeed sometimes just the council. These are bodies which are composed of distinguished Serbs from Bosnia, not necessarily members of the SDS, but whose expertise was made available to the SDS, and on which the leadership wished to draw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on in the chronology, Mr. Treanor, I'd like to ask you to identify any of the organs or bodies of which Mr. Krajisnik was a member.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, at the July assembly, at the latest, he was elected to be a member of the Main Board. In fact, at that assembly, he received a higher number of votes than any other candidate to the Main Board. He also later became a member of the Personnel Commission of the SDS, which was a body established by the Executive Committee, I believe, to consider the issue of the appointment of SDS candidates to government positions in BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you discussed the platform programme of the SDS. May I ask you now to turn to an interview with Radovan Karadzic in July of 1990, in which he elaborated some of the purposes and concerns of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interview which was published in the Belgrade news magazine Knin on the 20th of July, 1990. It's an interview that was conducted with him by one of the members of the editorial staff, Milorad Vucelic, who later went on to become the head of Serbian radio and television, and I understand today is still very active in the socialist party of Serbia

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Treanor. Your Honours, for the benefit of the Chamber and counsel, that may be found at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to the first highlighted portion, Mr. Treanor, which is found at page 6 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this interview, Dr. Karadzic goes over many of the same points that he made in his speech to the opening session of the SDS, and makes some other interesting remarks along the way. For instance, we see here him quoted as saying: "Our party has adopted the view of the Serbian nation in BH towards these questions. That is, remaining within Yugoslavia. Thus, the party is committed to a federal Yugoslavia, and within it a federal Bosnia-Herzegovina on an equal footing, with an unconditionally equal status for citizens and nations," again repeating one of the main points in their programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a small practical suggestion, which I hope would be helpful, and I don't think it will create any difficulty for the witness. That, for example, just at that point when the highlighted passage was identified as being at page 6, it would be exceptionally helpful, and I think would only take a moment and create no difficulty if -- well, either counsel or the witness were just to mention very briefly what the highlighted passage is. There is no problem obviously about his identifying it here. It's just that later reading the transcript, if there is simply a reference to page 6, it doesn't give an immediate clue as to the passage. Whereas with that little addition -- for example, in this case it's a numbered paragraph so that's easy, but a simple identification of the passage would make everybody's work subsequently on the transcript that much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger and Mr. Treanor, could you follow that suggestion, because it saves us not time at this moment, but later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we can turn to the next paragraph, which is numbered 38 in this translation, which states that in the event that demands for confederate, as translated, transformation of the country prevail, the Serbian nation in BH will, through its SDS, prepare its democratic response to that new situation as well. In any event, Serbs will not go along with living in some new independent state of Croatia, nor in any state in which their mother country, Serbia, is not included. That must be clear, so that there is no misunderstanding. And this is not because the party wants it, but rather because the Serbian nation demands it of its party." I made reference before to the proposals that Yugoslavia be transformed from a federation into a confederation. This was something that Serbian leaders in BH and in Serbia itself were against. So he is taking a position against that here. His reference to the independent state of Croatia refers to the state in Croatia which was set up under the auspices of Nazi Germany and fascist Italy during World War II, a state which engaged in a genocidal campaign against the Serbs in that state and that state did include Bosnia and Herzegovina. So here Dr. Karadzic is expressing the fears of Serbs about living outside of any state in which the rest of the Serbs are not also living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you indicated earlier the distinction between the platforms of the SDA party and the HDZ party with respect to the prospects of remaining within Yugoslavia. Does Dr. Karadzic, in this interview, address the -- any aspect of life, continued life in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This interview is interesting from that regard. The interviewer seems to be a bit surprised, for instance, that Alija Izetbegovic, who was the head of the SDA was present and indeed I believe spoke at the founding congress of the SDS in July 1990, and in this interview, Dr. Karadzic is at pains to emphasise the degree of harmony between the SDS and the SDA, between the Serbs and the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the previous passage indicated, much of his reserve, if I can put it that way, at this time is addressed toward the Croats. And if we could blow up the passage that's highlighted here, numbered 58, we can see him saying, in order to correct the views which the interviewer has identified in Serbia in regard to the Muslims, Dr. Karadzic says: "In Serbia, on the other hand, the press often wrongly refers to a fundamentalist threat in both Bosnia and Kosovo. It seems that this is done under the influence of certain Western European circles, who have their eyes fixed on Bosnia-Herzegovina as the European bastion of Islamic fundamentalism." So Dr. Karadzic is denying that type of threat in Bosnia and again in the interview emphasises the harmony existing between the Muslims and the Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that thought also continued on page 9 of the interview?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think if we look at paragraph 63 here, he states that: "Islamic fundamentalism is coming to Europe in the form of people of other races and other languages, and Europe is seized with panic. In our country, we have Muslims of the Slavic nation. People of our blood and language. The vast majority of whom are committed to the European quality of life, while preserving the Islamic faith. There is no place for panic here, neither among Serbs nor among Muslims."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, before we leave those pages, I wonder if either from counsel, and of course we'd accept any assurances there, or through the witness, we might seek some clarification of the status of the manuscript notes which have been made on this document and that the markings and particularly there is some writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask you because I noticed that next to paragraph 58 we find even some text. I couldn't read everything. It seems to start with "conspiracy."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It says: "Conspiracy --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether this is a conspiracy, isn't it. Could we get some explanation why we have an annotated version of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only state that the notes are not mine, and I really have no familiarity with this in principle, as I think I indicated yesterday; if I did not, I perhaps should have. I and my team work only with the original B/C/S of documents. It is only occasionally that we happen to see translations. Sometimes they are brought to our attention because people think there might be something that needs to be clarified. So I really cannot -- I think the only thing that I can say about this is I think this is -- the translation itself is a translation done by the FBIS, the Federal Broadcast Information Service, which is an American media monitoring agency. Where the -- and when the marginal notes were made, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that the original - I haven't got it in front of me - does not contain similar annotations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The original -- and I have an ERN copy here - is simply a Xeroxed copy from the pages of the magazine, and it contains no such notation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can clarify further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The annotations are in no way intended to communicate the views certainly of the witness or anyone within the OTP. To my understanding, this is the way the document was received and ERNed, but they can either be removed, or with that clarification the Court can understand that it is not intended to be part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this accepted by the Defence, or would you rather have a clean translation? Mr. Stewart, usually it's a disadvantage if you can't read something. Here it might be an advantage. I have difficulties in reading it anyhow, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do see what it says, but I'm not going to make an issue about this. We've seen it. If it becomes a major problem, if we see lots more of this sort of stuff, we might have to reconsider but at the moment we're not asking for any special steps to be taken, and I'm grateful for the clarification so far as it's been possible to give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, in the July -- in that July 1990 interview, Dr. Karadzic indicated that the determination of Bosnian Serbs not to live in a state in which their mother country was not included must be clear. Were concrete steps toward making that position clear to others in Bosnia and Herzegovina taken later in the year?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The next document illustrates that. And in moving to this document, I would also point out that at the very end of the interview, we just considered in its last sentence, Dr. Karadzic refers to the matter of outvoting. It says that something to the effect that on certain issues there can be no outvoting. I'm not sure how they translate that. This is an expression of the fear that he and the other SDS leaders had that even though the Serbs were a sizeable, indeed the second largest nation within BH, they did not form a majority, so that, therefore, it would be possible for, for instance, the representatives of the two other of the three largest nations to join forces and outvote them in a simple, straight-up vote in, say, the assembly or some other forum. This was something that they were determined to resist, and on the basis of the fact that they saw themselves, indeed defined in the constitution, as one of the constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore have a right to have all -- to have all decisions that affect them as a nation subject to their veto. Now, in the next document -- we just saw that paragraph. Thank you very much. The next document represents one effort to address that issue, which is a procedural issue perhaps, but one that gets to their fundamental political stand, that is, having the Serbs in BH remain within one state with all the other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document may be found at tab 9.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter signed by Dr. Karadzic under the letterhead of the Main Board of the SDS, and addressed to the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And to remind the Court, this is before the election, so this is the communist-dominated assembly, which is, in fact, about to be disbanded. And the letter refers to Articles - I'm sorry - Amendments 60 and 70 to the constitution. I referred to Article 60 yesterday. Indeed, it quotes Article 60, although it misidentifies it as Article 70, saying that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a democratic, sovereign state of equal citizens. The peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, and the members of other peoples and nationalities which live within it. Now, the premise of this letter is that the guarantees, the provisions of that Article have not been adequately addressed by that amendment, have not been adequately addressed by Amendment 70 to the constitution. Amendment 70 had changed the make-up of the Republic Assembly and had specified in its paragraph 10 that within the Assembly there would be formed a commission for the question of the equality of peoples. The letter see this as inadequate and suggests that another amendment be made to the constitution, which I think we have a blow-up of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, it's a practical matter. The -- looking at this particular document in English, it's a hard one to handle, because, as Your Honours will see, it starts: "Amendment seven, second character illegible, is not in concordance with amendment illegible. Amendment 7, second character illegible," and so on, which is quite hampering. The thing that's puzzling us is that when one looks at the B/C/S version, which I don't pretend to understand as language, but those characters are plainly not illegible. They are very easy to see. The numbering on the B/C/S version -- because in fact it should be: "Amendment 70 is not in concordance with Amendment 60. Amendment 70 reads," and so on. So there isn't in fact any difficulty, except that plainly we don't want to be faced with the task of constantly having to cross-refer to the B/C/S to get little clues as to the -- what the apparently illegible bit of the English version is -- is supposed to be saying. We're wondering if something can be done about this sort of document because it's absolutely unnecessary for the Tribunal and for us to be faced with something which makes continual references to illegibility, when there isn't apparently such a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I can tell you that the previous trial I presided, the Defence usually took a different position that whatever could be doubted was doubted as far as illegibility is concerned. So I can imagine that since the Translation Services sometimes are very much criticised for reading what some people think to be illegible, at other moments, they perhaps become overcautious. Because if you see these numbers, I would also say that it would be 70, but some people with some imagination might say that it's not for certain that it was not 78 and 60 not for certain could never be 80. So therefore, if we find ourselves in a position where we think that it's sufficiently legible by consulting the original text, I think this is the way we should try to solve it and I consider this, if the translation was made exactly from this copy, and if the copy is not darkened or made any lighter, then I would say that it is legible. If this often happens, we'll certainly ask the Prosecution to review whatever translations do exist in respect of illegible documents. So therefore, I do to some extent agree with you. On the other hand, I also do understand why our Translation Services have become perhaps sometimes overcautious and are not daring to read anything that someone could say is not for the full hundred per cent legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand that, and I'm very sorry that the translation team have been so intimidated by that previous fierce defence team. We, of course, are far gentler. But perhaps, Your Honour, we can approach it I think that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't understand the word "intimidation."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was not being that serious about it but Your Honour referred to their extreme nervousness about it. But, Your Honour, it seems the position is we can -- may we, with respect, keep this under review, then, to see if it emerges as a larger problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We hope that it's an exception rather than what will become a rule. And at least in explaining to us the document, Mr. Treanor has the original in front of him and easily read all the numbers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're about to blow up paragraph 4 in the document. Now again, to remind the Court, Dr. Karadzic in this letter is proposing a further amendment to the constitution, to the effect that the Assembly of the Republic establish three national councils or chambers within itself, a Serbian National Council, a Muslim National Council, and a Croatian National Council, composed of deputies from both assembly councils and chambers. Issue of interest for the realisation of the national equality in the Assembly of the SRBiH shall be decided in accordance with a separate procedure. The suggested amendment then goes on to specify the issues which the council would deal with. And then we can turn to the last paragraph in the document. Considering the constitutional arrangements and the Election Act, the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina are faced with two options for ensuring their equality as citizens and a people. First, the first option is contained in the proposal which we are now forwarding to you, and the second one is the declaration of the Serbian National Council," or a Serbian National Council. Now, the force of the act -- of the amendment which Dr. Karadzic sought would basically have given any one of the three constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina a veto over any measure before the Assembly which it felt adversely affected its interests as a nation. And among those issues, and indeed the first issue in the list, just under paragraph 4, item number 1, is the issue of the borders and the legal constitutional status of BH. In other words, it would have been possible for, under this proposed arrangement, for the Serbian deputies in that council to block the secession of BH from Yugoslavia. And Dr. Karadzic is saying that if this doesn't happen, the Serbian people in BH will take other steps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the date of the -- of this letter to the BiH Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th of October, 1990. And the elections are coming up on the 18th of November, to remind the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDS take steps toward the establishment of a national council shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not surprisingly, this letter did not draw favourable action, given that the Assembly was on its way out, and perhaps given the fact that the letter confused Amendment 60 with Amendment 70. So in fact, on the 13th of October, which is barely five days later, there was a large open-air meeting in Banja Luka to establish a Serbian National Council. Many Serbian politicians were present there from Bosnia and also from Croatia, giving very interesting speeches, and the assembly -- the assemblage voted to establish a Serbian National Council, and that council in fact made -- issued a decision on that day on certain issues. I think before we get to the decisions of the council, we can look at a portion, I think, of Dr. Karadzic's speech to that assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The transcript of the speech can be found in the intercepts binder at tab 1. Before we play a portion of that video, I would remind the interpreters that it is synchronised with the transcript and we therefore ask that no simultaneous translation take place. And Your Honour, I am reminded that the videos also require a separate number, were not previously numbered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be Prosecution Exhibit number P66, and the transcript of the video, P66A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours and counsel, the first clip of the video can be found at page 4 of the transcript, at tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next clip, please, which can also be found at page 4 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Treanor, we'll move on to the next clip.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I can comment on these two before we move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just going to ask that. In the first clip, the reference to former generals being elected presidents, something of that nature, is a reference to Franjo Tudjman, and in the second clip we see -- and the first clip also raises the spectre of civil war if the moves toward independence on the part of Croatia and Slovenia continue. In the second clip, we see the position of the SDS leadership on the republic boundaries. Just to remind the Court, the SDA was very much in favour of maintaining those boundaries. Here is the SDS position, stating that those boundaries are merely administrative boundaries and they cannot become state boundaries, which would divide the Serbian people among more than one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before moving on to the next clip, Mr. Treanor, any comments you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that clip, we heard Dr. Karadzic specifically addressing the situation in Croatia in the terms that I referred to earlier, that is, he said that if the Croats in Croatia wanted to leave Yugoslavia, that's fine, but they can't take the Serbs in Croatia with them. And then he moved on to address the situation in BH and raising the fear that the next step would be to try to take BH in its entirety, including the Serbs in it, outside of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the next clip, which may be found at page 5 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, any comments you wanted to make with respect to that clip from the speech?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here again we see -- or not -- first let me say that here we see now some fears expressed as to the positions -- the position of the Serbs in an independent BH, reference being made to the Turks, unfavourable reference, that is, to the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who are now perceived as a threat. And reference is also made to Assembly decisions which could appear legitimate, that is, the fear -- expression of the fear of outvoting, which I mentioned earlier. The majority of the Assembly could vote for the secession of BH and all of the Serbian delegates would be against that, but since they would not have a majority this would look perfectly legitimate to the outside world and this is what they were determined to prevent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you one question in between. Is my recollection right, that the reference to the Turks came from the republic and were not the words of Mr. Karadzic? Because you dealt with them in one line without making any distinction. You said reference is made and then you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could be the case. If we could play that again, we could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where the transcript says it came from the republic, I meant to say that it came from the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that clarify the Court's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It clarifies the issue. I think it would have been better if you would have made a distinction between the words of Mr. Karadzic and the words of those -- of individuals in the audience unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry about that, Your Honour. I'd just like to point out that, well, when he was referring to -- we saw what the -- what happened to the Serbian people before, even when they were a majority. That would have included a reference to the period of Ottoman or Turkish rule over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is not completely clarified on the transcript. It might be a good idea if the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- for the record, for the transcripts, confirmed the position as we now see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I must say, I don't remember the exact words, but where Turks were mentioned, the transcript of the rally of this meeting said that it was voices from the audience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. And Dr. Karadzic made no explicit reference to or use of the word "Turks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's clear enough, then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the next document, which may be found at tab 12. Did Dr. Karadzic, in his capacity as president of the National Council, issue a declaration on the position of the Serb people in BH?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have a declaration which -- I think we have skipped a couple of documents perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You referred earlier, I recall, to at least one decision by the Serbian National Council that you wanted to draw our attention to after we had viewed the rally.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was a decision on the formation of the Serbian National Council and a -- and then the so-called first decision of the Serbian National Council --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would turn the Court's --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would draw the Court's attention to tab 11 of binder 1.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can consider the second paragraph under the main heading in the document. This document is also dated the 13th of October and states that: "According to the decision of the Serbian National Council, the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall not recognise any decision to change the state character of BH taken by the deputies rather than the people, only a decision reached through a referendum of the Serbian people." So here the Serbian National Council is basically announcing at -- it is, in effect, setting itself up as the Serbian Chamber of Peoples, which Dr. Karadzic had earlier sought, and giving themselves a veto, so to speak, over any decisions made by the Assembly that would affect the interests of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the document you just referred to, the October 13th decision by the Serbian National Council, referred to a refusal to recognise decisions of that nature. Turning now to tab 12, declaration of the position of the Serb people. Does that suggest the possibility of actions beyond non-recognition in response to a declaration to which they were opposed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think if we turn to paragraph IV of that decision, a decision which bears the date of the 6th of November, 1990, we can see what the Serbian National Council is suggesting. "If a confederal solution or an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina should be imposed on the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbian people reserve the right to undertake actions as governed by the circumstances, in order to preserve their unity with the Serbian nation as a whole." And it goes on to say: "To this end, the Serbian National Council shall not acknowledge a single law or decision of the BH Assembly and state organs that is harmful for the interests of the Serbian people in BH, and the Serbian National Council shall arrange a plebiscite on essential issues of the national entity of the Serbian people in BH."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, several days later, Dr. Karadzic gave another interview to Knin. During the course of that interview, which may be found at tab 13, does he again touch upon or amplify upon the theme of actions to be taken in the event of decisions which threaten the unity of Serbs within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This interview was published in Knin, the same journal that the previous interview was published in. It was published on the 9th of November. The interview was conducted with the same journalist. And this is, in fact, the first interview in Knin after the previous one we saw. So it's sort of a continuation of that interview and it represents sort of a catching up on the situation in -- of the Serbs in BH for the readers of Knin. If we look at paragraph 4, there is a highlighted portion, beginning with the second-to-last sentence in that paragraph. In this section of the interview, Dr. Karadzic is referring to the success of the SDS in reviving political life among the Serbs in BH and the organisational work of the party. Again, I would remind the Court that this is only a few days, a week or so, before the elections are due to take place. And he states that: "Each member of a local board of the Serbian Democratic Party is in contact with 10 to 20 Serbian households, so that information from the most remote villages reaches the Main Board in two hours at most."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page 3 of the English portion of that interview. Does Dr. Karadzic during the course of the interview address the question of outvoting and possible responses to it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He returns to this issue again in the third paragraph from the bottom of the page. The second half of the paragraph is highlighted and reads: "The BH Assembly could become a place of dramatic events because the Serbs could be outvoted by a two-thirds majority regarding, for instance, the issues of the change of the state character of BH. Should that happen, all conditions for a civil war would be in place, because the Serbs in BH are no longer helpless, but very powerful and united. Everybody understands now that no political act can be completed here without the Serbs." Now we can move on in the article, on page 4 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that would be found at page 6 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we see, in the second paragraph from the bottom of the page, highlighted in English translation, a further statement: "The Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina will not give in so easily, and their freedom-loving political will, will be mobilised in the Serbian areas. The Serbian National Council will proclaim the rule of the Serbian people and undertake other activities and will ensure freedom for the people. Those who are preparing to rig the elections are playing with fire, which could scorch certain statehoods and certain sovereignties." Now, this statement, as the last part indicates, is made within the context of his discussion of fears that the communist power-holders in Bosnia who are in charge of running the elections will rig the elections and falsify the results and deprive the SDS and the other national parties of their rightful share and power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later in the interview, does Dr. Karadzic return to the theme of Serbs remaining within Yugoslavia and indicate what areas or territories among -- within Bosnia and Herzegovina are meant to be included?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if we turn to the next portion which we've highlighted on the last page of the translation, the first full paragraph at the top of the page: "Serbian priorities are the preservation of the spiritual, cultural, political, and state unity of the Serbian people. A Serbian priority is the return of the Serbian people among the happy peoples and the Serbian state among the happy states. A Serbian priority is preventing a single Serbian village from being left out of Yugoslavia and remaining in some new, independent state of Croatia." So here he seems to be claiming for Yugoslavia every Serbian village in Bosnia. Finally, at the very end of the interview, he states: "We are now openly saying what could not even be whispered before. The Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina pin all their hopes on their mother country, Serbia, and will never allow a state border to separate them from Serbia. Let all the peoples in Yugoslavia make their own arrangements regarding their states any way they wish. The Serbian people will do so too and will find a way to remain in the same state as Serbia, be it a simple or a complex one."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn quickly, then, to the next document, which is found at tab 14. Actually, the next two documents found at tab 14 and 15. Does this also reflect the theme of unity among the Serbs within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As Dr. Karadzic has now repeatedly said in the documents that we've considered, the SDS leadership is very determined that the -- all the Serbs in Yugoslavia remain in the same state and therefore he was interested in cooperating with Serbian political leaders outside of Bosnia. Here we see a letter addressed by him to Slobodan Milosevic on the occasion of his election as president of Serbia in the first direct elections to that office that took place in Serbia on the 9th of December in 1990. The two Articles that have been highlighted are the second and third from the end of the document, which Dr. Karadzic states that, in addressing Mr. Milosevic, "Your election means that expectations of the majority of the Serbian people in BH have been met, that one capable statesman with a great responsibility toward the state of Serbia towards all its citizens and toward all the Serbs outside Serbia becomes the leader of Serbia. Also through your electoral victory in the first free elections all to the last conditions have been met, which will ensure that Serbia and Serbs get full respect in the coming talks on Yugoslavia, also including the conditions for further strengthening of the relationship of Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina with their parent country Serbia." I could remark in connection with the responsibility of -- toward Serbs outside of Serbia, that that was in fact a provision in the new constitution of Serbia which was enacted in I believe September 1990, and in fact there was a ministry within the government of the Republic of Serbia which had special charge of the question of relations with Serbs outside of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next document found at tab 15, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter addressed by Dr. Karadzic to Milan Babic, who was the president of the Serbian National Council in Knin, which is in Croatia. So he is one of the main leaders of the Croatian Serbs. This letter is addressed to him on the occasion of the proclamation of a Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, that is, the Croatian Krajina. This event had taken place on the 19th of December, 1990. And we have the last paragraph there highlighted as of interest. "Along with the congratulations, accept our assurances that the Bosnia and Herzegovina Serb National Council will always be -- always by the spiritual, cultural, political, and state unity, also mean state unity of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina and all the other Serb regions with the Serbian mother country within a free, democratic, and federative Yugoslavia, regardless of its size." So here we have an expression of solidarity with the Croatian Serbs, who had the same desire as expressed by the leaders of the SDS, that the Serbs in Croatia should remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You wanted to move to your next subject or I saw you also looking at the clock. If these were your questions on these documents, there's one intermediary question by the Judges. Both letters, in translation, at least, bear no date. Is that true for the original as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Neither has a date, but they do have signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then clear. If this would be a suitable moment, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to adjourn for 20 minutes. We'll recommence at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you mentioned that the November 9th Knin interview with Dr. Karadzic took place shortly before the elections. Can you tell the Court about the results of those elections in BH.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We have to consider the elections that took place in the republic and the consequences of those elections before we can move into the next documents. I will address the results of the elections per se, and what those elections -- the results of those elections meant for the SDS as a party. First of all, the elections -- the elections took place on both the republic and the municipal level. There were primarily elections of deputies, I referred to them on the republic level or assemblymen on the municipal level, to the assemblies at those levels. At the same time, there were also elections to the Presidency of BH, which for the first time was being elected directly by the voters. Now, on the municipal level, to begin with those elections, we do not have available documentation which would give the summary results of those elections. However, Dr. Karadzic later stated before the SDS Assembly that the SDS had taken power in 37 municipalities, that is, had won a majority of the assemblymen in the assemblies of 37 municipalities. On the republic level, the elections to the two chambers of the Republic Assembly gave the SDS a considerable share of the seats. The SDS won the total of 72 seats, 38 seats -- if memory serves me correctly, 38 seats in the Chamber of Municipalities, and 34 seats in the Chamber of Citizens. The SDA, by contrast, won a total of 86 seats in those two chambers, and the HDZ, I believe, 44. Now, those two chambers were composed of, on the one hand, the 130 deputies in the Chamber of Citizens and 110 in the Chamber of Municipalities. One deputy for each municipality plus one for the city of Sarajevo. The total of 230 is important and, and considering the numbers in relation to that number is important, since, in accordance with Amendment 70 to the constitution, the Assembly could in many instances meet and make decisions in joint sessions, in which the deputies from the two chambers would sit together and combine their votes on particular measures, which are specified in that amendment, including, for instance, voting for the installation of the prime minister and the government. To get into a minor detail, in order for such a session to have a quorum, a majority of the deputies in each chamber would have to be present; however, the voting was done in a combined fashion. Then the elections to the Presidency also gave the SDS a share in that institution. According to the recent constitutional amendments in other legislation, the Presidency was to be composed of seven members. Two members were to come from each of the three constituent nations, that is, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats; and one was to be a -- of the Yugoslav nation, which was one of the ways that people could identify themselves for census purposes, for instance. All national identification in Yugoslavia is on the basis of self-declaration, I might add. So the Serbs were to get two seats in that Presidency, and in fact it was the two candidates of the SDS who were elected. They were Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. Just to round out the results of the election, I would mention the fact that the three national parties, even before the election, had got together and agreed to cooperate. I mentioned that -- we mentioned Dr. Karadzic's fear of electoral fraud on the part of the communists, the other national parties had a similar fear. So they agreed to form a coalition after the elections and agree among themselves on the -- on forming a government and distributing the posts within that government and the other posts that were available to them as victors of the election on both the municipal and the republic level. Pursuant to that decision, Alija Izetbegovic was elected as president of the Presidency for a term of one year, and Momcilo Krajisnik was elected president of the Assembly that took place on the 20th of December. And Jure Pelivan of the SDS [sic] was designated as prime minister, and his government, which contained representatives from all of the three parties, on the basis of an agreement which had been reached, took office on the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, excuse me. The transcript reads Jure Pelivan of the SDS has designated --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The HDZ. The agreement reached down through the municipal level and posts were apportioned there -- proportionately to the strength of the three parties in the particular Municipal Assembly, that is, the posts that were available would have been the president of the Assembly and then the members of the Executive Council of the Assembly, in effect, the municipal government. Now, as far as the SDS was concerned as a party is of course -- brought them to power. It gave them a lot of office-holders. And aside from the obvious fact that participation in government, it created a whole new group of individuals that were available to Dr. Karadzic and the other leaders of the party to consult with and to implement their policy through. Hitherto, the apparatus of the party, as we went over briefly earlier, consisted of the local boards, the SDS, headed by the municipal presidents of the SDS, and then there were the central boards, in particular, the Main Board and the Executive Board. Now we have Municipal Assemblymen who were SDS members, presidents of municipal assemblies; in effect, the mayors of the municipalities who were SDS members. Heads of Executive Councils who were SDS members or sympathisers, heads of the executive organs of municipal -- of the municipal executive boards. On the republic level, we now have ministers who are appointees of the SDS, if I can put it that way, not necessary members, but people designated by them to fill the posts allotted to them, as well as deputy ministers and other high-level functionaries within the government per se of BH. Then we also have, as I mentioned, 72 deputies in the Assembly of BH, who, as the other parties formed a Deputies' Club, which was an official body within the Assembly, the Deputies' Clubs of the various parties, and which became a forum for discussion of policy issues. So Dr. Karadzic now had available to him a much wider group of people than before, and people who were actually -- including people who are actually now in positions of power. And he in fact consulted with these types of people on a regular basis, sometimes on a one-to-one basis, but frequently in large meetings, where people from the various categories I described would all be present. We rarely find a meeting, if ever, a meeting of the Main Board itself, or just the Main Board members are present and do something. It's usually a much broader meeting at which municipal party presidents are attending, deputies, certainly members of the Main Board, ministers in the government. Now, one more observation in that connection is the fact that there is some overlap among these various groups of people. That is, I don't know, about 15 members of the Main Board were also deputies, including Mr. Krajisnik. Many of the municipal presidents of the SDS were also deputies. Many of them also occupied -- or may have occupied the position of president of the Municipal Assembly or president of the municipal Executive Board, depending on what job they thought might be more interesting. So this gave a new caste to the party structure. We don't see them operating strictly at the central level within, as I mentioned, the Main Board, but rather, having meetings attended by the various types of functionaries, two or 300 people sometimes, to discuss various issues and let Dr. Karadzic know what they're thinking and receive instruction from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can we turn, then, to tab 16, for the Court, and to the document which you'll see in front of you. And let me ask you if that document reflects some of the early experiences -- whether or not that document reflects some of the early experiences and responses of members of the SDS to the circumstances within the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very interesting document, both in itself and for the time period that it deals with. It is the diary of Mr. Maksimovic, who was the president of the Deputies' Club of the SDS, and he was also a member of the political council of the SDS, which was another one of those bodies that Dr. Karadzic could draw on and which various people belonged to. Now, in this excerpt and a couple of other excerpts we're going to see we'll see reflect the experience of being in this new coalition of the three national parties as seen by one of the top leaders of the SDS. And I think we have highlighted especially the first excerpt in the diary is the 3rd of January, 1991. Just to remind the Court: At this point in time, the new Assembly had been constituted and Mr. Krajisnik elected president of the Assembly, but the new government had not yet taken power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours and counsel, the excerpt from January 3, 1991 may be found at page 2 of the diary in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Treanor, does that refer to a meeting of one of the SDS bodies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This -- the entries in this diary are basically notes that were taken at sessions of the SDS political council. So this would be the meeting of the political council on the 3rd of January, 1991, a meeting about which otherwise we have no other available record, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the entry from January 3rd is highlighted, a particular portion at the bottom of the English translation of page 2, and at the bottom of the page which is shown on the screen. Can you tell us the relevance of that entry.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we see some of his reflections. "Do the new circumstances essentially change the basic political concept of the SDS? It is based on our wish that all Serbs live in the same state. We will never let them divide us up into states. Are we backing away from this important wish of our people?" He seems to be referring to the fact that now they've entered into a coalition government in BH, which to him appears a bit problematic, as we'll see in further entries. On the next page of the translation, at the -- starting with the second bullet-pointed entry, we see these thoughts: "What have our first parliamentary experiences shown regarding our national protection? We will have heavy fighting as deputies in the BH Assembly, with the Muslims and particularly the Croats and some communists and socialists as well. Forming new municipalities is difficult, because it will be difficult to have it approved by the BH Assembly. It will be the same with the forming of the Chamber of Peoples." These are two points which I would remind the Court came up in our discussion of the programme of the SDS and Dr. Karadzic's speech, the feeling that the municipal boundaries should perhaps be redrawn and the desire to, as we saw later expressed, to form a Chamber of Nationalities, to prevent outvoting. We move down a little bit in the middle of the page: "The present state of our unity is insufficient. We have heard many promises at meetings but what have we done? The unity of Serbian deputies has not been shaped. Some believe that the intellectual level of our deputies is satisfactory. However, our position in parliament will never be favourable. I am certain of that. There will be all sorts of things in the Assembly. Outvoting, treachery, rows walkouts, and protests. Is that democracy? We'll see." So again we have the fear of outvoting in the Assembly. And then we move down two bullet points to the entry: "Who says we can't create a Serbian state of sorts which will be more appropriate and bring us closer to the achievement of our immemorial ideals?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that's the last entry from that particular session of the political council?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I turned it off instead of turning it on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I believe that was the last entry from the January --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn now to the session of 17 January.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be found at page 6.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 6, at the third complete paragraph, we have highlighted an entry which reads, "my opinion." "Alija Izetbegovic is compromising himself too much as the president of BH. Muslim statements about Kosovo are very indicative and unacceptable to us. Efforts towards the establishment of the National Council should be stepped up and the Serbian National Council should be fully activated. I feel it is necessary that the SDS and the club of Serbian deputies in the BH Assembly be on the alert. People believe that Muslims and Croats are better organised in all respects. Weapons and illegal organisation. Complete conformity with the SPO, the Serbian renewal movement, should be established immediately. If Western Herzegovina is lost and belongs to Croatia, then we will not be naive and let go of Eastern Herzegovina. Can we rely on the JNA? How do we keep the Muslims with us? The Croats' stands are clear to me, but I fear treachery by the Muslims. Croats are our open enemies, but Muslims are sly, perfidious, and fickle enemies, always have been and will be. It will be too late if they catch us unprepared and history will be an unmerciful judge." I would just add that the reference to the SPO there in establishing cooperation with that party was in fact achieved. The SPO had elected one deputy to the Assembly and that deputy in fact joined the Deputies' Club of the SDS. The reference to Herzegovina is a reference to the fact that he perceives that the Croats in Western Herzegovina would like to split off from BH and join Croatia perhaps, and he expresses his fear for what may happen in the Serbian part of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question? Because I'm a bit confused. In the question, Mr. Tieger guided you to page 6, but previous to that he said: May I take you to the 17th of January. In the English text, I find this 17th of January indicated on page 3, no new date on page 4, and on page 5, I find the 24th of January. So I'm a bit surprised at what you've just read from page 6, would be part of the 17th of January, where I would expect it to be part of the 24th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies for what was obviously a misleading question. I thank the Court for clarifying that. I leave it to the witness, however, to view the document and make the appropriate clarification himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It does seem to be the 24th indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we have one more entry to consider at this point. On the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's found at page 8, although it appears the Chamber has found it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, this is also a political council session, as was the meeting on the 24th of January. And we read this entry: "My comments basically come down to the following: I am convinced that the Serbian deputies will not remain in the BH Assembly for long and that they will have to walk out, because we will not accept the adoption of any enactments against our will and approval which decide our fate. Attempts to dupe us into adopting the so-called declaration on sovereignty and indivisibility of BH was a very enlightening example for us." Now, the reference there is to an attempt to have discussed at a joint session of the Assembly at the end of January a declaration submitted by the -- a draft of which was submitted by the SDA on the sovereignty and indivisibility of BH which the SDS found unacceptable. On that occasion, at that Assembly session, it was decided to postpone consideration of that decision until the next session of the joint session of the Assembly, which in fact took place at the end of February. In the intervening period, a new draft, a new SDA draft, was produced, which was still unacceptable to the SDS, and the SDS Deputies' Club produced a document of its own, presenting its views on the future status of BH, which I think may be our next document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before moving on to that next document, Mr. Treanor, can I ask you one question about one of the highlighted portions of the January 3rd session. And that was the portion found at the bottom of page 3, I believe, of the English translation, in which Mr. Maksimovic discusses the possibility of forming a state which would be closer to the achievement of our immemorial ideals, and I wonder if you can shed light on the meaning of that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to speculate a bit here. He is certainly referring to the creation of a Serbian state of sorts. When he speaks of "our immemorial ideals," I'm not quite sure whose ideals he's referring to. He may be referring to the idea which is frequently referred to as a Greater Serbia, which in itself is sort of a indeterminate term. But basically, a state smaller than Yugoslavia, without the Slovenes, without the Croats, without perhaps - I say perhaps - Macedonia, but perhaps including Macedonia. Again, I'm not sure whose ideals he's referring to. But a state which would be territorially smaller than Yugoslavia, and therefore more heavily Serbian in population, but certainly encompassing the vast majority of all the Serbs who were living in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can turn to the next document found at tab 17. And I believe we'll find there the document produced by the SDS Deputies' Club, which presented its views and to which you referred earlier.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document dated the 14th of February, 1991. The month of February saw a lot of public discussion in connection with the draft decision and its forthcoming debate in the Assembly, and this document presents the views of the -- what we can see on the first page of the document is now referred to as the Club of Deputies, SDS and SPO, that is, Serbian Renewal Movement. It's again a fairly lengthy document, so let's move to a highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that may be found at page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 6 in the original, I believe. Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And here we see the statement that: "It is only within the borders of present-day Bosnia and Herzegovina, inseparable from Yugoslavia, that basic harmony of all the peoples can be achieved along with the conviction that none of the peoples in it will be subordinate or suppressed when it comes to determining our general fate. Our points of view are firm, even if some republics, for instance, Slovenia, Croatia, and Macedonia, completely secede from Yugoslavia and declare themselves independent. We repeat that the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina want to live even in a transfigured and even smaller Yugoslavia, which might not include some of its current republics." Now, here they are taking the position that they would like to see the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina remain within even a reduced Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we turn to tab 18 of the -- of binder 1, and the next document you selected, Mr. Treanor, do we find further iterations of the proposed boundaries or boundary issues related to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And before we consider this document, I'd just like to observe that in the debate in the Assembly on the 27th of February, it was decided, after much discussion, to end discussion about the draft decision. The draft essentially would have given the Assembly the right to consider its own enactments superior to those of the Federation and that type of thing the SDS found to be unacceptable as being basically a negation of the existence of Yugoslavia and its constitution. So a debate on that was ended. There was no vote. And -- however, this whole controversy had stirred up opinion. It was rather a polarising experience. And at the beginning of March, we see the SDS holding a mass rally in Banja Luka, at which its leaders publicly address the issues which have now been formally raised in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn, then, to the first portion of that document, which you've highlighted, which may be found on page 3 of the English translation -- I'm sorry. On page 2.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on the page in the translation, we see highlighted a portion beginning with the second sentence in the paragraph. This is a statement as quoted in the local Banja Luka newspaper, Glas, a statement by Milovan Milanovic, who was an SDS member of the Republic Assembly. He's quoted as saying: "On behalf of the humane people of Bosnian Krajina, we are sending word that any nation which is in favour of federal Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, could live together with the Serbs in this area. We already have a homeland, with Bosnia in it. We do not want boundaries along our alleys or streams, dividing brothers or neighbours. Those who want to leave Yugoslavia can have a pleasant journey but they should know that they will be allowed to take out of this country only what they have brought into it, and nobody can take Krajina from Yugoslavia without breaking their spine." Krajina is a rather large area in Western Bosnia which adjoins the Krajina area in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this particular rally took place in the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Banja Luka, which is the main town, if you will. It's not a city in the technical sense in BH. The main centre in Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn, then, to the remarks of Mr. Cizmovic, which are found on page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're at the very bottom of the page here. Mr. Cizmovic, speaking on behalf of the Serbian renewal movement, with whom, as I mentioned, the SDS having a combined Deputies' Club in the Assembly. Mr. Cizmovic is quoted as saying: "Today we address all Serbs, as we speak in the names of those who will never speak again. All Serb graves of this century, in Yugoslavia, bear the --" next page, "bear the signs of Yugoslavia. The Serb tree has cracked for the sake of unitary Yugoslavia's survival. We have never faced a greater risk. Out of the Serb people, other people have been formed. Out of the Serb faith, non-belief. Brotherly reconciliation is therefore the prerequisite of our times. The grandsons of the Chetniks and partisans must not repeat their grandfather's mistakes. The current borders exist only in the federal option. Hence, our placing the demand for the unification of all Serb lands." This is a statement very pregnant with meaning. The reference to peoples being formed out of the Serb people is a reference to the viewpoint of many Serbs that the Bosnian Muslims had in fact originally been Serbs and had -- were merely converts to the Muslim faith. Many Croats held a similar opinion, that they were in fact really Croats. The reference to the grandsons of the Chetniks and the Partisans is a reference to World War II, in which Serbs fought on -- within different armed formations in that war, the Partisans being the communist-controlled resistance movement and the Chetniks being a nationalist movement. And he again makes reference to the borders, that the current borders, that is, the existing republic borders, could only be considered valid if Bosnia remained within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask a very general question, Mr. Tieger. I wonder to what extent what we heard over the last, well, let's say, approximately the last hour, is in dispute between the parties.
